statement: In 166 healthy, screened adults aged 18 to 45 who took MDMA in a hospital research unit in Basel (nine double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover studies from one laboratory), a single dose raised blood pressure, heart rate and ear temperature above placebo in the same people over the next 6 hours. At 125 mg (136 people) the average highest systolic pressure was 157 mm Hg against 133 on placebo, the average highest heart rate 95 beats a minute against 76, and the average highest ear temperature 37.7 degrees Celsius against 37.4. Systolic pressure went above 160 mm Hg in 38 in 100 people against 6 in 100 on placebo, and above 180 in 5 in 100 against none; heart rate went above 100 in 33 in 100 against 2; ear temperature went above 38 degrees in 24 in 100 against 9 (editors' calculation: with MDMA, 32, 31 and 15 more in 100 people crossed the lines for systolic pressure above 160, heart rate above 100 and temperature above 38). The highest values were 196 mm Hg systolic, 145 beats a minute and 39.1 degrees; the paper reports no temperature above 40 degrees, no hypertensive urgency and no other sign of a hypertensive crisis (severe headache, shortness of breath, nosebleed). At 75 mg (30 people) the rises were smaller (systolic 145 against 131 mm Hg; temperature 37.2 against 37.0, not marked as significant); that comparison is between different people in different studies, and the difference between doses was significant for blood pressure but not for heart rate or temperature. Peaks came on average 1.7 to 2.4 hours after the dose. Laboratory studies from several groups, as summarized in a narrative review (second-hand), report a temperature rise that grows with dose (+0.1, +0.4 and +0.7 degrees on average at doses up to 1.0, 1.1 to 1.9 and 2.0 mg/kg), and one of 13 volunteers in an earlier study had a brief hypertensive crisis (240/145 mm Hg for 20 minutes). These sessions differ from real life: people rested, with a research assistant present, in a room at about 22.7 degrees Celsius; they took MDMA of known amount and no other drug, were healthy, four in five were new to MDMA, and no one took a second dose in the same session. Heat, dancing, crowding, other drugs, pills of unknown content and extra doses were not tested, and the study was too small to rule out events as frequent as 1 in 100 (for no temperature above 40 degrees in 278 sessions, the 95% interval runs from 0 to 1.3 in 100). Four people reported no effect of the drug and were left out of the analysis of when the felt effects began and ended; the paper does not say what their blood pressure, heart rate or temperature did. Everyone was given a fixed dose, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested here (controlled studies of a second dose are covered in separate claims); the authors, citing earlier studies, argue that effects fade while MDMA is still in the body (acute tolerance) and that adding more may not lengthen the effect but may add adverse effects, which is their reading and not a result of this analysis.
plain: In a hospital laboratory, healthy young volunteers took one dose of MDMA and, on another day, a dummy pill. With MDMA (125 mg in the study) their blood pressure, heart rate and ear temperature went higher than with the dummy pill. About 38 in 100 had a top blood-pressure number above 160, against 6 in 100 on the dummy pill; about 33 in 100 had a heart rate above 100, against 2 in 100; and about 24 in 100 had an ear temperature above 38 degrees, against 9 in 100. The highest temperature was 39.1 degrees. At a lower dose (75 mg) the rises were smaller, but that comparison used different people. The volunteers rested in a room at about 23 degrees with a staff member, took one pure dose and nothing else, and were healthy. Heat, dancing, crowds, other drugs and extra doses were not tested. Four people felt no effect; the study does not say what their bodies did, and nobody took more.
population: 166 healthy adults aged 18 to 45 (equal numbers of women and men; mean age 24.5; four in five new to MDMA), psychiatrically screened, mostly recruited on a university campus and paid, in nine studies at one hospital in Basel: 30 people in the 75 mg study and 136 in the 125 mg studies
exposure: A single oral dose of MDMA hydrochloride in capsules, taken at rest in a research unit with a research assistant present, room temperature 22.7 (SD 0.6) degrees Celsius (study conditions: 75 mg in 30 people; 125 mg in 136 people, 112 of whom took 125 mg a second time at least seven days later after a pretreatment medicine, a session not analysed here)
comparator: Placebo in the same people on another day (double-blind crossover); for the 75 against 125 mg contrast, different people in different studies
outcome: Highest blood pressure, heart rate and ear (tympanic) temperature in the 6 hours after the dose, and the number of people whose highest value crossed a clinical line (systolic above 160 or 180 mm Hg, heart rate above 100 beats a minute, temperature above 38 or 40 degrees Celsius)
magnitude: 125 mg (n = 136), average of each person's highest value in 6 hours, MDMA against placebo (SD): systolic 157 (15) against 133 (15) mm Hg; diastolic 93 (10) against 79 (8); heart rate 95 (17) against 76 (12) beats a minute; ear temperature 37.7 (0.5) against 37.4 (0.5) degrees Celsius; drug effect p < 0.001 for each. People above the line, MDMA against placebo: systolic >160 mm Hg 51 (38%) against 8 (6%); >180 7 (5%) against 0; heart rate >100 45 (33%) against 3 (2%); temperature >38 32 (24%) against 12 (9%). Highest single values: 196 against 175 mm Hg, 145 against 117 beats a minute, 39.1 against 38.7 degrees. 75 mg (n = 30): systolic 145 (14) against 131 (11); diastolic 84 (8) against 77 (5); heart rate 83 (17) against 69 (9); temperature 37.2 (0.3) against 37.0 (0.3), no significance mark; >160 mm Hg 3 (10%) against 0; heart rate >100 3 (10%) against 0; temperature >38 none. Dose-by-drug tests: systolic F 15.2 and diastolic F 17.9 (p < 0.001); heart rate F 2.38 and temperature F 2.43 (not significant). All 166 sessions: systolic >160 in 54 (33%), >180 in 7 (4%); heart rate >100 in 48 (29%); temperature >38 in 32 (19%); no temperature above 40 and no hypertensive urgency. Editors' calculation: at 125 mg, 32, 31 and 15 more in 100 people crossed the lines for systolic pressure above 160 mm Hg, heart rate above 100 and temperature above 38 degrees with MDMA than on placebo. Laboratory studies summarized in a narrative review: peak rise in core temperature +0.1 (doses up to 1.0 mg/kg), +0.4 (1.1 to 1.9 mg/kg), +0.7 (2.0 mg/kg).

evidence.locator: Methods > Study design, 1st paragraph; Methods > Subjects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods > Study drug, 1st paragraph (p. 577, left column into right column)
evidence.extracted: Pooled analysis of nine double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover studies, all at the University Hospital Basel, in 166 psychiatrically screened, healthy European or Caucasian adults aged 18 to 45 (mean 24.5, SD 4), mostly recruited on the university campus and paid, equal numbers of women and men. 30 people took a single 75 mg dose; 136 took 125 mg (24 once; 112 twice, once alone and once after another drug, at least seven days apart, the pretreatment sessions being analysed separately). This paper analyses the 166 sessions of MDMA alone against placebo. Exclusions: psychiatric disorder, physical illness, illicit drug use more than five times in a lifetime (past cannabis excepted), any in the last two months or during the study (urine tests before sessions). Fifty-nine people had tried a drug 1 to 5 times, 34 of them MDMA 1 to 4 times. The study drug was MDMA hydrochloride from a pharmaceutical supplier, in capsules.

evidence.locator: Methods > Pharmacodynamic measures, 1st paragraph (4 people left out of the timing analysis) and 2nd paragraph (p. 578, left column)
evidence.extracted: Four people reported no subjective drug effect and were left out of the analysis of when effects began and ended; the paper does not say what their blood pressure, heart rate or temperature did. Blood pressure and heart rate were measured in duplicate by an automatic oscillometric device after at least 10 minutes of rest, and temperature in the ear (tympanic thermometer), before the dose and at 0, 0.33, 0.67, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5 and 6 hours; in the 75 mg study the 0.33 and 2.5 hour temperature points are missing, and in one 125 mg study (24 people) the 2 hour point. Lines used: systolic above 140, 160 and 180 mm Hg; diastolic above 90, 100 and 110; heart rate above 100 beats a minute; temperature above 38 degrees Celsius (hyperthermia) and 40 (hyperpyrexia). The dose was not adjusted for body weight or sex.

evidence.locator: Results > Acute effects of MDMA on vital signs, one paragraph (p. 580, left column into right column)
evidence.extracted: MDMA alone raised blood pressure, heart rate and body temperature (Table 2). Over the 166 sessions: systolic above 160 mm Hg in 54 people (33%) and above 180 in 7 (4%); heart rate above 100 in forty-eight people (29%); ear temperature above 38 degrees Celsius in 32 (19%), up to 39.1. Highest values 130 diastolic and 196 systolic; no hypertensive urgency and no temperature above 40 (the highest among all 278 sessions, with or without a pretreatment, was 39.1). Systolic pressure, heart rate and temperature peaked on average 1.7 (SD 0.9), 2.0 (SD 1.4) and 2.4 (SD 1.2) hours after the dose. The mean room temperature was 22.7 (SD 0.6) degrees Celsius. A significant dose-response effect was found for blood pressure but not for heart rate or temperature; the shares above 160 mm Hg, above 100 beats and above 38 degrees were higher at 125 than at 75 mg (p < 0.01, p < 0.05 and p < 0.01).

evidence.locator: Table 2, 125 mg block (n = 136): blood pressure, heart rate and temperature rows, MDMA and placebo columns, and the Drug column (p. 582)
evidence.extracted: Average of each person's highest value in 6 hours, MDMA against placebo, mean (SD): systolic 157 (15) against 133 (15) mm Hg; diastolic 93 (10) against 79 (8); heart rate 95 (17) against 76 (12) beats a minute; temperature 37.7 (0.5) against 37.4 (0.5) degrees Celsius; drug effect p < 0.001 for each (F 486, 292, 267 and 44.4). People above each line, MDMA against placebo: systolic >160 51 (38%) against 8 (6%); >180 7 (5%) against 0; heart rate >100 45 (33%) against 3 (2%); temperature >38 32 (24%) against 12 (9%). Highest single values, MDMA against placebo: systolic 196 against 175 mm Hg; heart rate 145 against 117 beats a minute; temperature 39.1 against 38.7 degrees. Editors' calculation from the printed percentages: with MDMA 32, 31 and 15 more in 100 people crossed the lines for systolic pressure above 160 mm Hg, heart rate above 100 and temperature above 38 degrees than on placebo.

evidence.locator: Table 2, 75 mg block (n = 30): blood pressure, heart rate and temperature rows, MDMA and placebo columns (p. 582)
evidence.extracted: Average of each person's highest value in 6 hours, MDMA against placebo, mean (SD): systolic 145 (14) against 131 (11) mm Hg; diastolic 84 (8) against 77 (5); heart rate 83 (17) against 69 (9) beats a minute; temperature 37.2 (0.3) against 37.0 (0.3) degrees Celsius, the temperature difference carrying no significance mark in the table. People above each line, MDMA against placebo: systolic >160 3 (10%) against 0; >180 none; heart rate >100 3 (10%) against 0; temperature >38 none against none. Highest single values, MDMA against placebo: systolic 176 against 153 mm Hg; heart rate 134 against 95; temperature 37.6 against 37.7 degrees.

evidence.locator: Table 2, the Drug x dose columns (F and p); Results > Subjects' interest in using MDMA again, 1st paragraph (p. 582)
evidence.extracted: Drug-by-dose interaction (the 75 against 125 mg contrast): systolic F 15.2 and diastolic F 17.9, both p < 0.001; heart rate F 2.38 and temperature F 2.43, both not significant. The 75 and 125 mg groups are different people in different studies. Average highest temperature on placebo was 37.0 (SD 0.3) in the 75 mg study and 37.4 (SD 0.5) in the 125 mg studies. Four in five of the participants had never taken MDMA before, and the rest had very limited experience (at most four earlier exposures).

The authors read the vital-sign changes, in people at rest, as similar to moderate physical activity; transient systolic pressure above 180 mm Hg was seen in 5% of those given 125 mg, with no other sign of a hypertensive crisis (severe headache, shortness of breath or nosebleed); an earlier analysis of 74 people from laboratory studies had found systolic pressure at or above 160 in 32% and at or above 180 in 9%. Temperatures did not rise above 39.1 degrees Celsius. No controlled clinical study of MDMA has reported a temperature above 40, which the authors suggest may be because participants had moderate single doses at rest, were well hydrated and were not in a hot or crowded place, unlike some recreational settings.

Onset of effects 33 minutes, peak 1.6 hours, duration 4.2 hours; the 75 and 125 mg doses did not differ in how long effects lasted. The authors attribute the short duration of effect, compared with the long time MDMA stays in the blood, to acute pharmacological tolerance, so that effects decline while MDMA is still in the body, and argue that adding more MDMA might not relevantly prolong the effect and may increase adverse effects (citing a separate study of second doses). This is their interpretation, not a result of this study: every session used a fixed dose.

evidence.locator: Discussion > 'The present safety data' paragraph (research assistant) and 'The present study has limitations' paragraph (p. 585, right column)
evidence.extracted: A research assistant was always present with the participants in the laboratory, similar to a therapy session. Only psychiatrically healthy, mostly young people were included. Blood sodium was not assessed. The sample (166 sessions of MDMA alone, 278 with or without a pretreatment) was too small to exclude infrequent (0.1 to 1%) or rare (under 0.1%) adverse events; with no temperature above 40 degrees Celsius in 278 sessions, the 95% interval allows up to 1.3%.

evidence.locator: Table 1, the 'Overall Mean' rows (p. 3); Section 8 > Overview, 1st paragraph (p. 7, right column)
evidence.extracted: In the review's table of placebo-controlled laboratory studies (several research groups; 4 to 16 volunteers per study; oral, ear, armpit, swallowed-sensor and rectal temperatures; doses given per kilogram or in mg), the peak rise in core temperature averaged +0.1 degrees Celsius at doses up to 1.0 mg/kg, +0.4 at 1.1 to 1.9 mg/kg and +0.7 at 2.0 mg/kg. The review says the rise was related to dose, with low doses having minimal effects. Second-hand: a narrative review of small studies, not read in the original.

evidence.locator: Section 2 > Body temperature in laboratory studies, paragraphs on Vollenweider et al. (1998) and Mas et al. (1999) (p. 2, right column)
evidence.extracted: As summarized by the review: of 13 volunteers given 1.7 mg/kg by mouth (Vollenweider and colleagues), one had a brief hypertensive crisis (240/145 mmHg) lasting 20 minutes; in 8 men with earlier MDMA experience given 75 mg and 125 mg (Mas and colleagues) the peak rise in temperature was +0.4 degrees Celsius at both doses, about 2 hours after the dose, the review being unsure whether the peak was significant.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 is high overall on the card only because of the 75 against 125 mg contrast (different people in different studies, not randomised). The MDMA against placebo comparison in the same people, on which the claim rests, is at worst some concerns: the order of sessions is not described, blinding probably did not hold at 125 mg, some temperature time points are missing, and about 60 outcomes were tested without correction. The main outcomes are device readings and the effects are large (F 44 to 486), so one level, not two.

inconsistency.note: Nine studies from one laboratory agree; laboratory studies from other groups, seen second-hand, agree in direction for temperature. The dose difference is significant for blood pressure and not for heart rate or temperature, which the claim states.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for healthy, screened volunteers at rest in a cool room and says that heat, dancing, crowding, other drugs and extra doses were not tested.

imprecision.note: 166 people; the 125 mg comparison with placebo separates clearly (SDs and F tests). The 75 mg group is small (30) and is described as such; no intervals are printed.

publication_bias.note: Nine registered studies, one unpublished, pooled by the team that ran them; no sign of selective omission.

grade.reasoning: Placebo-controlled double-blind within-person laboratory studies start high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1 (see the domain note); inconsistency, indirectness as worded, imprecision and publication bias 0. Moderate for the statement that a single dose of 125 mg raised blood pressure, heart rate and ear temperature above placebo in healthy volunteers at rest. The shares above each line are descriptive: they count people whose highest of many readings crossed a line, and 9 in 100 placebo sessions also crossed 38 degrees, so the lines show how many people went over them and not a threshold of harm. The 75 against 125 mg contrast rests on different people in different studies and is not tested for heart rate and temperature; the paper's abstract and Conclusion call all three shares significantly greater at 125 mg, and this claim follows the tests instead. Status replicated by the same team: nine studies, one laboratory and one analysis model; other groups are seen only second-hand through a narrative review. The claim gives no advice, does not say whether the changes are harmful, and does not generalise to settings that were not tested.

verification.flag_note: Other groups' laboratory studies (Vollenweider 1998, Mas 1999, Tancer 2003, Freedman 2005, Kolbrich 2008) have no reference record here and are seen only through a narrative review (Parrott, 2012); the pooled studies share one laboratory, hence replicated by the same team. The paper's Conclusion calls single-dose MDMA safe in healthy people in a controlled setting, which is broader than its data (heat, activity and crowding excluded; events under about 1 in 100 not excluded); the claim does not use it. The paper's recommendation of a fixed dose for women rests on comparing different studies and is not used. Table 2's 75 mg and 125 mg blocks come from different studies with different placebo temperatures (37.0 and 37.4). The repeated-dose laboratory studies are covered by the library's separate claim on repeated doses.
